g.text: C332 · Keeping the laser off-chip: the case for external sources (§8.1)

text.style: font-size: 8.4px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #a1a1a6

g.text: Treat the laser like an “optical power supply” that sits outside the silicon chip. Advantages (2)–(7) from the book — advantage (1), the thermal budget, is in the previous lesson.

g.text: The fibre route is already in commercial products:

text.style: font-size: 7.6px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #f6f6f6

g.text: e.g. TeraXion’s coherent receiver uses an external laser

text.style: font-size: 7.6px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #f6f6f6

g.text: as the local oscillator, mixed with the received signals.

text.style: font-size: 6.8px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #a1a1a6

g.text: (local oscillator = reference light the signal is compared with)

text.style: font-weight: 700; font-size: 8.4px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: middle; fill: #f6f6f6

g.text: Takeaway: off-chip lasers avoid the insulating BOX and CMOS-foundry concerns, and bring mature III-V parts, WDM sources, isolators and PM fibre — a cost analysis decides.

text.style: font-size: 7.4px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #a1a1a6

g.text: Source: Chrostowski & Hochberg, Silicon Photonics Design §8.1 (p.295–296), advantages (2)–(7) + cost analysis; file.md l.13671–13685.

text.style: font-size: 7.4px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #a1a1a6
